articles.text: Thanksgiving is almost here, and with it comes the 23rd Annual Piedmont Turkey Trot. The 5K run through Piedmont streets will take place on Thanksgiving morning, November 28 at 8:30 a.m. with the start and finish line located at the Exedra on Highland Avenue. The race has received 1300 registered entries and organizers anticipate that number to double by race day. Runners will be coming for more than 100 cities from cities as far away as Arlington, Virginia and Calstock Cornwall, England. Race rewards include a turkey for the overall men’s race leader and overall women’s leader, plus a pair of running shoes from Transport. Winners in each age division will receive a pumpkin pie, courtesy of Piedmont Grocery, a cap and a bouquet of flowers from J. Miller Flowers. The top three runners in each age group will also receive cards for Yellow Door café in Montclair. The 2024 race shirts, hats and swag bags have been delivered, with shirts in purple for the first time in over a decade. Race Shirt Pickup On Wed. Runners may pick up their race bibs the day before the race, Wednesday afternoon November 27, between 3:00-6:00 p.m. at the Veterans Hall. Dog bandanas will also be available during this time for $6. The first Tiny Tot Trot for children ages 3-6 will be taking registrations from 3:00-4:00 p.m. and their race will take place at Witter Field on Wednesday at 4:15 p.m. It will be a 1-2 lap race around the track. Race proceeds benefit Piedmont High School’s cross-country and track & field teams, as well as the PHS Boosters Club. They also benefit Piedmont Middle School’s cross-country and track teams, and the Piedmont Junior Running program led by Leonard Goldman. Race director Sandy Proctor said, “We are all squared away. We have our city permit in place. We’ve worked with the police and the fire department and City Works… Our sponsors are all lined up and they’ve got their signs ready to go, so it looks like it’s going to be a great year.” Entry fees are unchanged from last year: • Adults 13 & older: $50 • Children 12 and under: $30 Register at Piedmontturkeytrot.com Runners at the front of the pack at the last year’s Piedmont Turkey Trot.

His sense of wonder was not misplaced for historians of the era such as Flavius Josephus and Tacitus commented on its beauty. Jesus, however, gave a shocking response. He informed everyone who was listening, “Before long, it will all come tumbling down.” When they were out of the city and looking at the temple grounds from the Mount of Olives, Jesus explained his comments to the leaders of his disciples. “Hard times are coming. It will seem like the world is coming apart at the seams. The scale of human suffering will be immense. Yet, mark my words, this is but the beginning of the birth pangs. This low point will be a turning point.” How can this be? How can our low points be turning points? It may be that low points can be turning points because they cause us to turn anew to the only one who can tell us who we are, the only one who can teach who we are born to be, the only one who holds us when the world breaks us, the only one who stills us when our foundations shake. Long before Jesus, long before there was a temple at Jerusalem, maybe even long before there was a Jerusalem, there was a woman of deep faith named Hannah. Hannah was broken. In a world that defined women by their ability to have children, Hannah did not have a child. She went into her temple at the old city of Shiloh and prayed earnestly, yet silently, for a son. The priest at the temple, Eli, observed her and rebuked her. “Go home. You are making a spectacle of yourself. Look at you. Drunk in a sacred space.” This low point for Hannah proves to be a turning point. Her longing to give birth serves as the birth pangs for a new way of being. Editor: I am writing to express my support for the proposed EV charging station at 29 Wildwood Avenue and to commend the Planning Commission’s recommendation to limit its hours of operation from 6 a.m. to 10 p.m. This restriction, especially from the perspective of nearby residents, strikes a reasonable balance between community needs and maintaining neighborhood peace. I also appreciate the plan for an 8-foot soundproof wall along the property perimeter to help reduce noise impacts on adjacent homes. However, I am concerned about the effectiveness of relying solely on off-site camera monitoring to manage on-the-ground issues. During the Planning Commission meeting, Shell representative Matthew Lyons was unable to outline a specific plan to address safety concerns, disturbances, and noise. Without a clear, proactive management strategy, these issues may place an undue burden on nearby residents. Approving the Conditional Use Permit (CUP) without a comprehensive on-site plan or reliable off-site monitoring would be like driving with blinders on. If it’s true that this is one of few rapid EV charging stations in a low density residential area, then it’s in everyone’s best interest that the operation of this one doesn’t exert undue burden on the local community. From my perspective, neither the risks nor rewards for Piedmont citizens of a 24/7 operation have been adequately addressed. The potential site security risks can’t really be addressed due to the fact that there are no current Shell EV charging hubs in the US. Similarly, there’s no consistent information on the anticipated usage of the EV charging hub by Piedmont residents. I recall that during the meeting on Oct. 28 a Shell employee stated that the expected usage of the EV charging hub would be around 40 cars a day. At the same meeting, proponents of 24/7 estimated that as many as 1000 Piedmont residents who, as emergency medical workers, could potentially benefit from overnight EV charging hub services. articles.text: A book drive for the East Bay Children’s Book Project (EBCBP) will be held at the Piedmont Turkey Trot bib pickup on Wednesday, November 27, from 3:00-6:00 pm at the Veterans’ Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue. Volunteers will be collecting new and gently used children’s books, including board books. Books should be clean with no marks or stains. No textbooks, religious books, encyclopedias, magazines, adult books, or library discards please. Bring donated books in boxes for easy transport to EBCBP. The mission of EBCBP is to help build literacy by putting books into the hands of children who have little or no access to them. Working through individuals and organizations who help children in need, the organization has given out more than 2,000,000 free books since opening their doors in 2005. School Board and City Council members started this tradition more than 10 years ago. EBCBP volunteer and former Wildwood Elementary School librarian Ellen Reed notes that 570 books were donated last year during this event. “We are so grateful for the community’s contribution to our children’s literacy project year after year,” said Reed. Volunteers are needed to help receive donated books on Wednesday, November 27, from 3:00- 6:00 pm, and drive books to EBCBP at 2501 Harrison Street in Oakland. Those with an interest in maintaining this tradition are asked to e-mail Sarah Pearson at srpear@gmail.com. If you miss this opportunity to donate books, you may drop off books at EBCBP on Tuesdays 3:30-5:30 pm or on Saturday, December 7, from 10:00 am-1:00 pm. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Pool has been taking some steps forward in construction and planning with the electrification of the pool by PG&E. Now more than one year behind schedule, the pool is expected to open next Spring. The Pool Advisory Committee held its first meeting since April 2022 on Thursday, November 14 at City Hall. Electrification for the pool began with the installation of a transformer on Saturday, November 9 and connected by PG&E on November 16. The community pool was initially approved by residents who voted for a budget of $19.5 million as Measure UU in November 2020. At the time it was scheduled to open in summer 2024. Based upon the most recent changes in July 2024, the pool budget has swelled to $32 million and an opening in Spring 2025. The Pool Advisory Committee, consisting of Sarah Olsen Meyes, Carolyn Pan, and Steve Roland, began the recent meeting with the introduction of a new committee member, Marcia Lane, and a review of information on the pool’s design and construction history. Paula Cooper-Tipton was introduced as the city’s new Aquatics Recreation Supervisor. Tipton has extensive experience in aquatics, including 8 years as aquatics coordinator for the city of Richmond. Public Works director Daniel Gonzales provided details about the construction process as well. As of now, the competition pool has been excavated and tile work has been completed. Pool construction was stalled early by the presence of ground water and the discovery of two buried fuel tanks. Waterproofing has been completed. Work on the smaller activity pool will start within the next two weeks and is estimated to take about three weeks to complete. Checking all systems will take 2-3 months. The Pool Committee disA PG&E engineer connects the transformer for the pool on November 16. cussed types of pool passes for when the pool opens, pass benefits, guest passes, and resident discounts. Proposed guidelines would focus on prioritizing residents and local sports programs, defining clear hours of operation, and avoiding the need for subsidies in operating costs. The committee also spoke with Stu Isaac, president of Isaac Sports Group, about the keys to success for the community pool project. Isaac outlined the need for financial stability, well trained staff and a wide range of concurrent programming. For financial management, Isaac assured the committee that he would give budget projections and promised budget accountability. Resident Stacey Rodel spoke to the committee, asking if there would be any plans to include programming for masters swimming with the community pool. Isaac responded that there is time in the pool schedule to consider time to rent the pool to a local masters team, and her input was supported by committee member Marcia Lane. During closing announcements, committee member Steve Roland commented on the next PAC meeting. “I encourage everybody to come and please speak up. There’s going to be a bunch of different models. A lot of data. I’m actually concerned about being overwhelmed by the amount of data… And it’s going to be really important to have public input, from every possible constituency of the town, to give us as much information as we can.” The Community Pool Advisory Committee will meet next at 6:00 p.m. on December 10, at City Hall. The Committee agenda will plan to discuss Pool Pass Models and Operating Budget Projections. Pool Advisory Committee member Sarah Olsen-Meyes (left) with new committee member Marcia Lane. Once he is comfortable with a new person, which doesn’t take long, Peanut is affectionate, trusting, and a loyal companion. He is happiest being close to people and likes to rest his big head on laps or lean in for pets. You can see an adorable video of him getting a bath on the shelter’s website. Although he is strong, he doesn’t pull when walked on a leash, making for pleasant strolls. Peanut attends dog playgroups and his ideal home would either be with another mild-mannered dog or as the only dog. articles.text: The Piedmont Education Foundation’s (PEF) Giving Campaign has launched a new fundraising challenge called “Pop Up Participation.” It has set a goal of raising $4,000,000 and receiving donations from 75% of all families. Giving Campaign chairs Catie Osborn and Kim Hunter have announced that if 75% of families participate in the Giving Campaign the entire town will enjoy a community-wide pajama day. A chart by Mulberry’s Market is tracking progress so the city can watch as Piedmont works toward the ambitious target of 75% participation. “Imagine our whole community celebrating with a pajama day with even our city officials in their PJs!” said Osborn. “It’s a fun and lighthearted way to recognize the serious difference each donation makes, no matter the size.” PEF reminds the community that participation by residents is vital to supporting Piedmont schools and that donations signal a united commitment to bettering the education system for all students. articles.text: It’s the giving season once again – that time of year when we exchange gifts and consider charitable contributions to nonprofit organizations that enhance our quality of life. Did you know there is science behind giving? It turns out that the human species is hardwired to help others. It’s part of our survival instinct according to psychologists, neurologists and anthropologists. Giving also makes us feel good by releasing endorphins, those chemicals produced by our brains to improve our mood, reduce pain, etc. You could say that making a charitable contribution feels as good as eating a plate of seasonal favorite cookies or a warm hug from a loved one. Psycholog y Today has reported on what it calls “The Happiness Trifecta”. Eva Ritvo, MD, writes, “Helping others triggers a release of oxytocin, which has the effect of boosting your mood and counteracts the effects of cortisol (the dreaded stress hormone). Interestingly, the higher your levels of oxytocin, the more you want to help others. When oxytocin is boosted, so are serotonin and dopamine!” It works at any scale, and everyone can do it. “When most people think of giving, they may have too narrow a focus,” according to Ritvo. “All giving works A donation box is located in the Chabot Space and Science Center atrium. wonders, not just cash given once or twice a year. How can you help others? Is there a cause you support? A friend that needs help? A stranger that needs a random act of kindness? You should fill every day with small acts of giving, as this is an effective way to bring happiness to yourself and others. Even just smiling at someone is an act of giving and will brighten both of your days.” This holiday giving season, be generous with your cash, your volunteer time and your kindness. articles.text: On October 19, the 8th grade Piedmont Girl Scouts Troop 33587 went on their first overnight backpacking trip of the school year to Redwood Regional Park. They set up camp on Friday after school and immediately started preparations for dinner. At the start of the season, the troop welcomed three new members from a former Beach Girl Scout Troop. For some it was their first backpacking trip. The Girl Scouts planned and cooked Korean bulgogi and banchan for dinner. Additionally, the girls reviewed the “leave no trace” principles and discussed a project the troop will be completing this year to earn their Silver Award, which is given for outstanding community service and is among the Girl Scout’s highest honors. On Saturday the girls hiked down a trail near the camp to a small redwood grove before packing up and hiking out. This is the eighth year that Troop 33587 has had Scout adventures. Four members have been in the troop for all eight years. The troop has plans for future camping trips and projects like the Silver Award, with the possibility of attempting to earn the Gold Award next year, the highest honor in Girl Scouts. Over the years the troop has participated on organizing trash pickup and recycling for Wildwood Elementary School, and selling enough cookies to earn a VIP trip to Disneyland. articles.text: Staff Photos Inara Mehta with a forehand smash in her No. 3 doubles win over Marin Academy. Piedmont High’s girls’ tennis team finished their post-season on Friday, November 15, after losing to No. 4 No. 4 Marin Academy 5-2 in the North Coast Section team tennis championships. As the No. 5 seeded school, the Highlanders opened with a dominant 6-1 win over No. 12 Urban of San Francisco at home at the Corey Reich Tennis Center. After a rain-out on Thursday, PHS wound up hosted the next day in the loss to the Wildcats. “We had a good win over Urban and only lost one match. We had some close matches against Marin Academy, but could only win one match at singles and one match at doubles,” coach Jim Landes said. Against Marin Academy, the Highlanders battled to a 2-2 draw through the first four matches, but the Wildcats won the remaining three matches. Of the wins was at No. 3 doubles with Inara Mehta and Abigail Call, winning in three sets, 6-3, 4-6, 6-1. The match was Piedmont’s second win of the afternoon, which drew the Match Day at two apiece. “It’s very exciting to get an NCS win, but we still need those two more. It kind of puts you on the edge, but its great to get one of the wins for the team,” Call said. Call and Mehta won their first set but dropped the second before turning in a dominant 6-1 in in the third set. “Abby played great in the first set and was picking everything Abigail Call in her No. 3 doubles win against Marin Academy. up. Second set was closer, but we took the shots we could in the third set,” Mehta said. “We played Marin Academy before and we played really well, so I expected us to get a win. I think we got a little rushed in the second set and we just wanted to finish the third set quickly,” Call said. The loss to Marin Academy essentially ended the Highlanders’ tennis season aside from the D2 NCS Individual Tournament on Monday and Tuesday, November 18-19. Looking ahead to 2025, Piedmont will graduate No. 1 singles starter Carolina Romanczuk, No. 1 doubles starter Emma Eisemon, along with Alina Shahid and Call. articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ soccer team got its season started with a successful scrimmage against San Leandro on Thursday, November 14 at Witter Field. Piedmont outscored its opponent 4-1, though no official score is maintained in scrimmages. The Highlanders demonstrated their usual counter pressing and fluid action under new head coach Ben Russell in his season debut. “We’ve only had three sessions and just one on a full-sized fields. So running in bigger spaces is something we’re going to have to understand a bit more. We had some cramps, but the key components were the counter press and managing the game,” Russell said. While former coach Todd Sullivan was known for his vocal and exuberant demeanor on the sideline, Russell is the opposite – only using his voice when needed. “My sister had coach Russell when she was a senior and she only had good things to say about him,” said PHS senior Gianluca Bini. “I’m psyched to have him as a coach. He’s an absolute phenomenal coach.” The first goal could be a sign of things to come. Niko MarkoGianluca Bini sends in one of his two goals in a scrimmage with San Leandro. Niko Markopoulos sends an assist to Gianluca Bini. Staff Photos New boys’ soccer coach Ben Russell makes his Piedmont debut. poulos sent a cross from a free kick to Bini at the far post for a header goal and a quick 1-0 lead. . “We needed a right-footed player to send that ball in and I just tried to look for the tallest guy,” Markopoulos said. “We have a lot of big players and when we get set pieces and corners, we’re going to put the ball in the box to our tall players. When you have a fantastic player like Niko, we’ll be able to put the ball in the right spot,” Bini mentioned. It was a dominant night for the Highlanders, recording 15 shot attempts with eight on target. “Overall, it was a really happy first game with the boys. The fact we were able to work on two different formations was really impressive. We can see the areas we want to develop and understand,” Russell said. PHS got its season officially started on Tuesday against Campolindo. They look ahead to hosting Oakland Tech on Thursday, November 21. Match Recap After recording four shot attempts, including a header on target by Bini after receiving a pass from Markopoulos, Bini scored the game’s opening goal in the 21st minute after Markopoulos whipped in a pass from a free kick about seven yards outside the penalty area. Bini then scored again in the 34th minute when goal keeper Lucas Malecki launched a pass from Piedmont’s own box past midfield to Bini—who retained the ball after a faulty tackle by San Leandro, dribbling by the approaching keeper to slot in a shot in the 28th minute. San Leandro got one back in the 37th, making it 2-1 at halftime. Piedmont took just two minutes to score in the second half when Logan Faucher assisted Bosco Lorin for a goal in the 42nd. Lorin and Markopoulos also had shots on target in the 51st. PHS then scored by way of an own goal in the 63rd after sending in a long pass from a free kick, leading to the final 4-1 score. Final stats: Bini scored two goals. Markopoulos and Faucher had assists. Lorin scored once. Piedmont outscored its opponent 4-1, though no official score is maintained in scrimmages. The Highlanders demonstrated their usual counter pressing and fluid action under new head coach Ben Russell in his season debut. “We’ve only had three sessions and just one on a full-sized fields. So running in bigger spaces is something we’re going to have to understand a bit more. We had some cramps, but the key components were the counter press and managing the game,” Russell said. A woodpecker at Redwood Regional Park. Stream Trail from the Canyon Meadows Staging Area are bushels of ladybugs. Scientists determined that their behavior is a mechanism for the species to reproduce and cope with a limited food supply during the winter months—laying eggs on the underside of leaves. The Stream Trail is predominantly flat, so it’s a great location for children and senior walkers. To reach the location, there are a few options. For an easy walk, start at the Canyon Meadow Staging Area off of Redwood Road and take the Stream Trail which starts at the end of the parking lot. At 1.5 miles you’ll reach a bridge and intersection with the Mill Trail. Take the bridge to continue down the Stream Trail and .2 of a mile later you will encounter the swarms of ladybugs. Turning around from this point will end your day at slightly over three miles of hiking. Should visitors want to experience more of Redwood Regional and add a workout to their visit, park at the Redwood Bowl Staging Area off of Skyline Boulevard. Take the West Ridge Trail until it intersects with the Madrone Trail, traveling left. You’ll walk slightly less than a half-mile until reaching the Starflower Trail, which you will take all the way until reaching the Stream Trail about 0.8 mile away. From there, you’ll walk about a half-mile to reach the ladybug swarm. Returning to the Starflower Trail and hiking back to your car will take about 1.6 miles and top out your day around 850 feet in elevation gain. Another option is taking the Redwood Peak Trail and walking uphill to Redwood Peak—taking 1.2 miles from the ladybugs. Redwood Peak is possibly the best hidden treasure of the park, where you can find a collection of boulders with initials, names, and dates etched into its surface. It is a great location to relax and hydrate while you scour the boulders to find the oldest date. The oldest year I was able to find went all the way back to 1918. It’s worth mentioning that the Stream Trail is one of the most popular trails at Redwood Regional due to the ladybug swarm and the general easiness of the walk. On a Sunday around 11:00 a.m., we passed approximately 122 people on the Stream Trail as we made our way to the Tres Sendas Trail. On the Tres Sendas and Starflower Trails, we passed just 20 people on the way to Redwood Peak and passed another 41 people while on the West Ridge Trail. The Chown Trail was one of the most secluded and perhaps the most underrated, passing just six people in the mile descent. Back on the Stream Trail, we passed another 51 patrons while making our way back to the car for a total of 240 park-goers we encountered on the trails. The Stream Trail provides a staggering 173 of those numbers alone. The collection of boulders at Redwood Peak has names, initials, and dates from several generations etched into its surface. articles.text: The San Francisco Ballet’s 2024-25 season begins on December 6 with the holiday favorite Nutcracker, honoring the company’s legacy as the first in the nation to present a full-length production. This special production is set in San Francisco’s post-1906 earthquake era, with opening scenes featuring famous landmarks like the Painted Ladies at Alamo Square. Nutcracker is the longest-running production in the company’s history. San Francisco Ballet premieres the production every year and features a cast of more than 150 dancers to tell the classic story of the Sugar Plum Fairy. Artistic Director and principal choreographer Helgi Tomasson’s production is inspired by the city of San Francisco, accompanied by an orchestra performing Tchaikovsky’s familiar score. Photo of a past production of The Nutcracker by San Francisco Ballet A diverse array of instruments are played during performances, including a glockenspiel, triangle, suspended cymbal, crash cymbal, tambourine, snare drum, bass drum, castanets, tam-tam, ratchet, and timpani – all played by only three musicians. Sasha De Sola will dance the role of the Sugar Plum Fairy, and Jasmine Jimison and Fernando Carratalá Coloma perform the roles of the Queen and King of Snow. Scenic design is by Michael Yeargan and costume design is by Martin Pakledinaz. Performance times vary. Visit https://www.sf ballet.org/productions/nutcracker/ to purchase tickets.

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Gardens’ annual holiday fundraiser and festival, Garden of D’Lights, begins this Friday, November 22. Garden of D’Lights is a fun outdoor holiday lights experience in Walnut Creek that is suitable for all ages. The event is even petfriendly, but keep in mind that all pets must be leashed. Thousands of lights and lasers transform the Garden’s cacti, succulents and trees into magical, multicolored botanical sculptures, unlike anything else in the East Bay. The holiday light and laser show highlights the 3-acre garden and its many succulents, cacti, and native flora. The gardens house plants from various hemispheres, so there is always something in bloom at Ruth Bancroft. articles.text: Oakland Zoo opened its gates to nighttime visitors this week for the fifth year of Glowfari, the illuminated lantern festival. The nocturnal event lets the zoo animals rest out of view but lets visitors view hundreds of all-new and larger than life animal lanterns. Walking through the displays of beautifully glowing lanterns gives off a feeling of Disneyland’s Main Street Electric Parade. The Rides Area is open too, as is the gondola to the top and the Express Train to Wild Australia. This year’s display features all new themes, as visitors are transported on Africa’s longest river, the Nile, to view wading wildlife and ancient Egyptian structures. Glowfari will also have a down-on-the-farm feel as guests will see lanterns of barnyard favorites cows, sheep and chickens. The zoo’s winter wonderland will be enhanced by a visit from Santa Claus. who will be stationed in the Rides Area on weekends in November and every night from December 1 to 23 from 6:00-8:45 p.m. Glowfari also will be open on select days in January. Purchase tickets in advance. Re-entry is allowed until 8:30 p.m. Oakland Zoo is located at 9777 Golf Links Rd, Oakland, 632-9525. Visit Oaklandzoo.org for more information. articles.text: Visit the Conservatory of Flowers in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park on December 14 and learn how to make an ornamental holiday wreath under the mentorship of a local artist. articles.text: Father-son photographer duo featured in Fort Mason exhibit Museo Italo America in San Francisco presents “Elio & Stefano Ciol: Into The Light,” an exhibit showcasing the work of Italian father-son photographers Elio and Stefano Ciol. Both photographers, hailing from Casarsa della Delizia in the Italian region of Friuli Venezia Giulia, are known for works that highlight their masterful use of light, balance of geometric lines and angles, and impeccable photographic composition. These three essential aspects enabled the father-son pair to create visually captivating and highly structured pieces that stand the test of time. Elio, born in 1929, lived his formative years during Nazi occupation and is renowned as one of the foremost European masters of landscape photography. Many of his predominantly black and white shots have been featured in more than 100 solo exhibitions. The current exhibit includes a collection of photos spanning more than 60 years. The exhibit is at the Fort Mason Center for Arts & Culture, 2 Marina Blvd, in San Francisco, and will be on view through February 2, 2025. Museum hours are Tuesday through Saturday, 12:00 p.m. to 4:00 p.m. and Sunday, 10:00 a.m. to 2:00 p.m. The museum is closed on major holidays including Thanksgiving Day, Christmas and New Year’s Day. The exhibit is free on Thursdays. Museo Italo Americano is the first museum in the United States devoted exclusively to Italian and Italian-American art and culture, located in San Francisco’s historic Fort Mason. articles.text: Bosch and Bosch Legacy are two episodic series streaming on Prime, and based on the acclaimed novels of Michael Connelly (City of Bones, Echo Park and The Concrete Blonde). At the center of the stories is homicide detective Hieronymus (aka Harry) Bosch, assigned to the LAPD Hollywood Division. To follow this character in the novels is to form an image of the man, his style, his way of being. To be introduced to him in Bosch/ Bosch Legacy only adds a new dimension to his fictional persona. He is perfectly portrayed by Titus Welliver who is experienced, often abrasive, and laconic in the extreme. These qualities are not off-putting but well played as Harry moves in a world that is raw, gritty, and often deeply dark. As well, Bosch must carefully navigate the political/bureaucratic maze of the hierarchical LAPD. Nothing about him is a cliché. In the opening of Episode one he and his partner J. Edgar (Jamie Hector), are following a suspect. Fearing they will lose him, they split up (against department policy), and Bosch proceeds on foot, following the man down a side alley. It’s the middle of the night, and all is shadowed and obscured. The suspect, appearing from the back of a dumpster, confronts Harry, pulls a gun from his jacket pocket but is shot by Bosch. The narrative cuts to a courtroom two Titus Welliver as LAPD Homicide Detective Harry Bosch years later where Harry and the department are involved in a civil suit over fatal shooting. And so begins the many episodes that introduce a panoply of characters as well as setting up Harry and J. Edgar’s next case regarding the possible murder of a young boy whose bones are discovered in the hills of Laurel Canyon. As Bosch and J. Edgar gather evidence, visit the crime scene, interview those who are in some tangential way connected to the skeletal remains of the boy, they encounter a panoply of ancillary participants. Harry spends time on site with a medical examiner (Alan Rosenberg) who is also a philosopher of sorts. The doctor engages Bosch, asking the detective how he deals with the spiritually harrowing world he confronts daily, his days a perpetual reveal of the damage people inflict on one another or themselves with a finality that is all but inexplicable. This reality is a through line connecting Bosch and Bosch Legacy. In the aggregate this is superb storytelling, unremittingly hardedged, grim, and can’t look away watchable. If you enjoy wellmade, character-driven police procedurals, you will be solidly entertained by these two series, and likely wish for a Season 3. Bosch and Bosch Legacy. Television series (crime drama). Streaming on Prime. Core cast: Titus Welliver, Jamie Hector, Amy Aquino, Madison Lintz, Lance Reddick. Rated TV-MA.

articles.text: Broken Embraces was written and directed by Pedro Almodovar, the best-known and most successful Spanish filmmaker of the last four decades. His most memorable film, at least in the U.S., was Volver (Return), and starred, as does Broken Embraces, Penelope Cruz, often referred to as Almodovar’s muse. It is unusual for male directors to explore and celebrate the resilience of women and their will to survive and even prevail. Volver is about women, young and old, women who are buffeted by the vagaries of life, by the inexplicable and by the unexpected. The narrative is compelling as are the complex characters. Broken Embraces is a love story with a strong woman at its center: the stunningly beautiful Elena (Penelope Cruz), who does what she must to carry on, to help her parents, even it means working as a discrete call girl and a secretary for a wealthy industrialist. Gradually she is pulled into a web of intrigue and duplicity and the film takes on a noirish tone as it moves from 2008 to 1994 in revealing flashbacks. The film is also completely taken with the transformative face of Elena/Cruz. She is shown in tight shots, pouting, smiling, making love, dressed in a variety of stylish clothes, at times looking like Audrey Hepburn or Marilyn Monroe. No doubt the camera loves Cruz and she loves it back. There are moments in the film when it feels like a Vogue layout so lovely is she photographed. But as a story, constructed around intense relationships, a story that is convoluted and multilayered, it feels strangely detached as if Almodovar cannot quite penetrate an abiding distance, perhaps because he is telling three stories simultaneously: one in 1994, another in 2008, and a third derived from the fact that there is a film within the film. Surprisingly, there are few if any moments in Broken Embraces when the characters reflect on the meaning of their actions. They are undisturbed by their choices and the narrative simply glides along in an undemanding way based on the assumption, presumably, that the filmgoer is not interested in knowing anything about the interior motivations of the characters. It is a missed opportunity by Almodovar to build intimacy with the audience. And so, though all is revealed, little is revealed. Even when the film is set, briefly, on two islands, Ibiza and Lanzarotte, Almodovar seems inclined only to use the lush scenery as a mere backdrop for Elena and her lover, Harry Cain (Luis Homar) and not as an extension of the heat of their relationship. Clearly Almodovar doesn’t believe in foreplay. If you love movies and have followed the career of Pedro Almodovar – or perhaps you saw Volver and were charmed by the power and intimacy of the women, or taken with a filmmaker who clearly loves to tell stories about wonderful women of all types – then Broken Embraces is a film not to be missed. Or if you simply love movies and are tempted to see a film by an artist like Almodovar who consistently struggles to convey the elusiveness inherent in exploring the human condition. Broken Embraces. Starring Penelope Cruz, Luis Homar, Lola Duenas, Blanca Portillo and Angela Molina. Written and directed by Pedro Almodovar. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated R. Streaming on Fandango/prime/apple tv. By Chris Honoré Bosch and Bosch Legacy are two episodic series streaming on Prime, and based on the acclaimed novels of Michael Connelly (City of Bones, Echo Park and The Concrete Blonde). At the center of the stories is homicide detective Hieronymus (aka Harry) Bosch, assigned to the LAPD Hollywood Division. To follow this character in the novels is to form an image of the man, his style, his way of being. To be introduced to him in Bosch/ Bosch Legacy only adds a new dimension to his fictional persona. He is perfectly portrayed by Titus Welliver who is experienced, often abrasive, and laconic in the extreme. These qualities are not off-putting but well played as Harry moves in a world that is raw, gritty, and often deeply dark. As well, Bosch must carefully navigate the political/bureaucratic maze of the hierarchical LAPD. Nothing about him is a cliché. In the opening of Episode one he and his partner J. Edgar (Jamie Hector), are following a suspect. Fearing they will lose him, they split up (against department policy), and Bosch proceeds on foot, following the man down a side alley. It’s the middle of the night, and all is shadowed and obscured. The suspect, appearing from the back of a dumpster, confronts Harry, pulls a gun from his jacket pocket but is shot by Bosch. The narrative cuts to a courtroom two Titus Welliver as LAPD Homicide Detective Harry Bosch years later where Harry and the department are involved in a civil suit over fatal shooting. And so begins the many episodes that introduce a panoply of characters as well as setting up Harry and J. Edgar’s next case regarding the possible murder of a young boy whose bones are discovered in the hills of Laurel Canyon. As Bosch and J. Edgar gather evidence, visit the crime scene, interview those who are in some tangential way connected to the skeletal remains of the boy, they encounter a panoply of ancillary participants. Harry spends time on site with a medical examiner (Alan Rosenberg) who is also a philosopher of sorts. The doctor engages Bosch, asking the detective how he deals with the spiritually harrowing world he confronts daily, his days a perpetual reveal of the damage people inflict on one another or themselves with a finality that is all but inexplicable. This reality is a through line connecting Bosch and Bosch Legacy. In the aggregate this is superb storytelling, unremittingly hardedged, grim, and can’t look away watchable. If you enjoy wellmade, character-driven police procedurals, you will be solidly entertained by these two series, and likely wish for a Season 3. Bosch and Bosch Legacy. Television series (crime drama). Streaming on Prime. Core cast: Titus Welliver, Jamie Hector, Amy Aquino, Madison Lintz, Lance Reddick. Rated TV-MA. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Cars 3 To the delight of young audiences, Pixar’s wonderfully animated cars (the equivalent of Hot Wheels), are characters with large, expressive eyes (the windshield), a mouth/voice (cum grill) and are emotive in all the right ways (anthropomorphic). And so this brings us to Cars 3, and the return of Lightning McQueen (Owen Wilson), racecar extraordinaire. We quickly learn that McQ. has had a hard crash and the world of racing waits to hear whether the legendary winner of the Piston Cup will return to the track. But as the veteran racers quickly learn, things have changed: hard-core rookies have come onto the scene who aggressively feel the need for speed. As a result, some of the familiar denizens of the track have retired. Some of the car sponsors are taking a serious look at the new hotshots such as Jackson Storm (Armie Hammer), and they wonder if the newbies will take the lead in the up and coming racing teams. McQ., however, is still a big name in the racing world (despite a narrow loss to Storm), and is encouraged by his friends such as Mater (Larry the Cable Guy) and Sally (Bonnie Hunt) to not step away, knowing how much McQ. Loves the rush of racing and competing, which still beckon. In other words, McQ. is game, but also realizes that he’s feeling some wear, noting that his tires, for example, are a bit bald. Luckily, Mcq. finds a rich sponsor-billionaire named Sterling (Nathan Fillion) who is a little skeptical, wondering if the legend still has the right stuff to win. To hedge his bet, he assigns his trainer Cruz Ramirez (Cristela Alonzo) to give McQ. some support. Plus there’s the guidance in spirit of Doc Hudson (the late Paul Newman) and his old pit crew chief, Smokey (Chris Cooper). Together, the gang sets out to prove that McQ. can still cross the checkered flag finish line first. Kids will root for McQ. Plus the animation is Pixar perfect, as always. Cars 3. Directed by Brian Fee. With voices of Owen Wilson, Cristen Alonzo, Armie Hammer, Chris Cooper. Walt Disney – Pixar. 1 hr., 49 min. Rated G. articles.text: The Secret of NIMH is a wonderful, compelling story, both whimsical and thrilling, its handdrawn animation is extraordinary, rich in detail and color, and follows in that familiar tradition in which animals talk and reason. It was adapted from the 1971 children’s classic, Mrs. Frisby and the Rats of NIMH, written by Robert C. O’Brien. From the opening set up, the narrative is flooded with a sense of urgency that fully engages the young audience. Mrs. Frisby (Elizabeth Harman), a widowed mouse, lives with her two children in a cinder block located in an open field on the Fitzgibbon farm. She learns that the field is soon to be plowed and she must move her family as quickly as possible to a safe place. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, November 20, 2024 Walking on Wednesday Wednesday Walkers visit Bear Park on King Ave. By Dick Carter Nearing the end of 2024, the Walking on Wednesdays group realized they hadn’t been to King Avenue this year, so that was last week’s destination. The walkers went up Highland to Sheridan Avenue and then up Lincoln to King Avenue, where ginkgo trees with striking yellow leaves lined both sides of the street. Native to East Asia, they are considered the oldest specie of tree in the world. The group went down King enjoying its lovely homes whose construction was spread out over the first half of the last century. The group stopped at 84 which was built in 1910. From Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s research, it was shared that Wallace Alexander, who has been called “Piedmont’s Philanthropist,” built a threestory mansion at Sea View and Hampton in the first years of the 1900s and a carriage house that is now the home at 84 King. Across the street from it is Crocker Park. The land for it was purchased by a group of neighbors headed by Alexander. By 1917, the City was making improvements to make the land into a city park, but the Key System extended their #10 line to what is now the Hall Fenway and Crocker Park, and it acquired a right of way for its electric streetcars. From 1912 to 1956, this right of way ran on a straight diagonal path through the park from the Hall Fenway to the corner of King and Hampton. Two rows of Canary Island Pines were planted along the way, and what is left of them line up in a pair of lines through the park. A few years back, one of them fell on Hampton Road during a strong windstorm. The streetcars stopped operating in 1956 and AC Transit used the right of way briefly to park buses. When this stopped, Herbert Hall bought the right of way land. He built the Japanesque house at 90 Crocker in 1961 and gave the deed for the right of way to the City. In his deal with the City, Hall negotiated the right to keep his pool equipment garage on a small portion of the land. This garage has the same Japanesque design as the house. Since 1972, the Piedmont Beautification Foundation has contributed to the landscaping, planting, and maintaining the iron benches in the park. A granite sculpture of a smoothly rounded bear and her two cubs by Beniamino “Benny” Bufano sits in the park’s center. Bufano was a California-based Italian American sculptor and known for his large-scale monuments representing peace. This Bufano Bear was installed by the Piedmont Beautification Foundation in 1978, and the cobblestone base is a memorial to Marie Veitch who lived nearby. The walkers continued down King to La Salle Avenue. Just before La Salle there is a wonderful, exotic front yard garden. On a past walk the group met the homeowner and he told them the story of the garden’s creation. It was originally a typical Piedmont grass front yard, but he had an inspiration. A neighbor was doing an excavation and had a truckload of dirt that he was willing to trade for a case of beer. The mound of dirt provided the base for this large tropical plant garden. Jim Kellogg and Mike Henn were on the Piedmont Planning Commission at the time and Jim told the walkers about the challenging approval process for the unusual landscape design. It started out with a 10’ hill but was reduced to 5’ after a “ballistic” neighborhood reaction to the plan. The walkers agreed the garden turned out to be wonderful. The group made their way to the end of King at La Salle and turned up it. A PG&E crew was replacing a 1954 AT&T power poll just before Crocker Avenue. The walkers navigated their way around the closed street and made their return to the Exedra. They passed the lower end of Crocker Park and went through the Hall Fenway with a new understanding of this beautiful part of Piedmont’s history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join. There is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required and can be done at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu, or by calling 510 420-3070. Comparing these two locations “is like comparing apples to oil drums,” said resident Rick Schiller. In their response time, Shell claimed that the charging equipment would be “virtually silent”, with noise only produced by cooling fans while equipment was drawing maximum energy in very hot weather. Shell also pushed back against requests for a bathroom, claiming that it would be a security risk with no regular on-site worker present.
